problem: Human evaluation of social robot navigation needs human input, but modern robotic simulators are compute-heavy rich-client desktop apps that cannot be run in a crowd worker's browser. HRI crowdsourcing has therefore been limited to passive video surveys, or to hand-built WebGL re-implementations.
motivation: Social robot navigation has no agreed evaluation protocol, and its social aspects are subjective, so scalable human feedback is required. Interactive online simulation could bring remote participants closer to real human-robot interaction than videos, at crowdsourcing scale.
key_idea: Run an unmodified rich-client simulator on remote Linux servers, share its GUI with each user's browser via VNC (noVNC), and use a reverse proxy, a Process Manager and a load balancer to scale to many concurrent users.
insight: Sharing a desktop GUI works for any Linux simulator without porting to WebGL, and it supports ROS dependencies, which WebGL export cannot. Startup is 18.9 s on average, versus over 2.5 min just to download a 1.5GB WebGL world. The interactive-vs-video study shows perceived robot competence and social-norm compliance differ between the two modes, and interactive surveys felt less mentally demanding. Video surveys may therefore not give the same perceptions as interactive ones, though the causes were not tested.
method: VNC-based GUI sharing: the simulator runs on a remote server, TurboVNC (with VirtualGL for GPU rendering) serves its GUI, and noVNC + websockify shows it in the browser and passes keyboard input back.

Process Manager (Flask): receives requests carrying a user ID and simulation parameters, launches a per-user session (simulator, ROS in Docker, VNC server and client), redirects to the user's VNC page, and shuts sessions down after a configurable time limit.
NGINX reverse proxy: routes HTTPS requests by URL path to the Process Manager or a user's VNC client, so the connection is encrypted and no extra ports are exposed.
Horizontal scaling: an AWS Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions distributes users across multiple GPU hosts (NVIDIA T4), with no shared state between hosts.

SEAN-EP instantiation: the SEAN Unity/ROS social navigation simulator with Rocketbox avatars, a third-person WASD avatar interface, a Kuri robot driven by the ROS Navigation Stack, and Qualtrics survey integration through iframes; interactions are logged as ROS bags.
Study design: 6 interactive simulations (find the robot, follow it for 30 s, reach a landmark) in a warehouse and a lab. A paired video-survey condition uses recordings of the interactive sessions.

setting.backbone: none (systems paper; the robot uses the classical ROS Navigation Stack with layered costmaps)
setting.observation: third-person rendered simulator GUI streamed to a browser; the robot uses simulated 2D LIDAR + odometry
setting.action_space: keyboard WASD control of a human avatar; robot uses ROS Navigation Stack velocity commands
setting.simulator: SEAN (Social Environment for Autonomous Navigation, Unity + ROS)

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results; only system performance and human-study statistics, so nothing goes in the benchmark schema.
results: SEAN-EP served 62 participants. With multiple hosts it collected 31 responses in 1.5 h, versus about 8 h on a single host (81% faster). Only 23 of 372 trials timed out (6.18%), and startup averaged 18.9 s. Compared with video, interactive sessions gave lower robot Competence (median 3 vs 3.83, p<0.0001) and lower mental demand (median 2 vs 3, p<0.01). Discomfort showed no significant difference.
limitations: Evaluated on only one simulator (SEAN) and one robot and navigation scenario, with a third-person avatar view; no comparison against real-world interactions.
Multi-host scaling adds management overhead, and some participants behaved undesirably (about 18% pushed the robot, about 12% collided with a human).
The reasons for the interactive vs video differences are untested, and no first-person view or display-type controls were used.
compares_to: Robot Management System / Robot Web Tools
